reviewedFields: reference title, URL, kind, and reading note
scope.method: Read every article in full before editing. Rechecked niche claims in primary papers and official technical documentation. Authored one original, topic-specific three-paragraph source-reading section per article. Executed arithmetic and small algebraic/finite-difference checks in V8; validated on-disk JSON, topic coverage, prerequisite IDs, section uniqueness, reference schemas, and source-reading lengths.

enrichment.wordCountConvention: Whitespace-delimited words in added section paragraphs; titles excluded.
enrichment.approach: Source-specific reading questions, original toy calculations, counterexamples, diagnostics, and explicit assumptions/trade-offs. No invented paper section numbers or reproduced extended passages.

issues.before: The same numerical timestep can represent very different noise levels under different schedules. In a variance-preserving process, ᾱ_t controls the remaining signal variance and 1 − ᾱ_t the noise variance. Their ratio is a useful measure of prediction difficulty. Early high-signal states preserve image detail, while late low-signal states require stronger reliance on the learned data distribution and conditioning. The schedule decides how training and sampling traverse these regimes.
issues.after: The same numerical timestep can represent very different noise levels under different schedules. In a variance-preserving process, ᾱ_t and 1 − ᾱ_t are the squared signal and noise coefficients. For unit-variance data and independent standard Gaussian noise, they also give the two variance contributions. Their ratio is the conventional signal-to-noise ratio. Early high-signal states preserve image detail, while late low-signal states require stronger reliance on the learned data distribution and conditioning. The schedule decides how training and sampling traverse these regimes.
issues.reason: State unit-data-variance assumption and distinguish coefficient SNR from actual signal variance.

issues.before: SNR(t) = ᾱ_t / (1 − ᾱ_t)
issues.after: Conventional SNR(t) = ᾱ_t / (1 − ᾱ_t); actual variance ratio = ᾱ_t Var(x₀) / (1 − ᾱ_t) for independent unit-variance noise
issues.reason: State unit-data-variance assumption and distinguish coefficient SNR from actual signal variance.

issues.before: At what ᾱ value is the variance-based signal-to-noise ratio equal to one?
issues.after: At what ᾱ value is the conventional signal-to-noise ratio equal to one?
issues.reason: State unit-data-variance assumption and distinguish coefficient SNR from actual signal variance.

issues.before: ᾱ/(1 − ᾱ) = 1 implies ᾱ = 0.5. Signal and noise each contribute half the variance under this convention.
issues.after: ᾱ/(1 − ᾱ) = 1 implies ᾱ = 0.5. With unit-variance data and independent standard Gaussian noise, signal and noise each contribute half the variance.
issues.reason: State unit-data-variance assumption and distinguish coefficient SNR from actual signal variance.

issues.before: Define pT(i)=exp(zi/T)/Σj exp(zj/T). A common distillation objective combines ordinary label loss with T² KL(pteacher,T || pstudent,T). The T² factor compensates for the gradient scaling introduced by temperature under the standard formulation. Both teacher and student distributions must use the same temperature for this comparison. For logits [2,0], the first-class probability is about 0.881 at T=1 and 0.731 at T=2, illustrating how relative alternatives become less suppressed.
issues.after: Define pT(i)=exp(zi/T)/Σj exp(zj/T). A common distillation objective combines ordinary label loss with T² KL(pteacher,T || pstudent,T). The T² factor compensates for the leading high-temperature gradient scaling under the standard formulation; it does not make gradients exactly invariant at every temperature. Both teacher and student distributions must use the same temperature for this comparison. For logits [2,0], the first-class probability is about 0.881 at T=1 and 0.731 at T=2, illustrating how relative alternatives become less suppressed.
issues.reason: T² temperature compensation is asymptotic; centered-logit matching remains informative at high temperature.

issues.before: Post-hoc temperature calibration fits a temperature on held-out validation data to adjust confidence. Distillation temperature shapes training targets. Generation temperature changes which tokens are sampled. They use related mathematics but optimize different goals. Tune temperature without looking at test outcomes, and report the mixture weight between hard-label and distillation losses. Extremely high temperature can make targets nearly uniform and weaken useful distinctions. A soft distribution is informative only when its relative probabilities carry relevant structure.
issues.after: Post-hoc temperature calibration fits a temperature on held-out validation data to adjust confidence. Distillation temperature shapes training targets. Generation temperature changes which tokens are sampled. They use related mathematics but optimize different goals. Tune temperature without looking at test outcomes, and report the mixture weight between hard-label and distillation losses. At high temperature, probability differences shrink, but T²-scaled distillation retains a centered-logit matching signal in the limit. Nearly uniform targets therefore do not imply vanishing information in that scaled objective; which distinctions help still depends on the task and teacher.
issues.reason: T² temperature compensation is asymptotic; centered-logit matching remains informative at high temperature.

issues.before: The accumulated gradient is four times the intended combined-batch mean gradient. This changes the effective update and interacts with clipping, optimizer state, and regularization; it is not merely a logging difference.
issues.after: The accumulated gradient is four times the intended combined-batch mean gradient. Under plain SGD this gives a four-times-larger step at the same learning rate. For Adam, a constant positive rescaling of the entire gradient history largely cancels between first and second moments, apart from ε; changing scale midway or introducing clipping and coupled regularization can break that cancellation. Normalize explicitly instead of assuming every optimizer responds identically.
issues.reason: Gradient magnitude and optimizer step magnitude are distinct; Adam's scaling cancellation has historical consistency assumptions.
issues.origin: Claude baseline suggestion independently validated by OpenAI

issues.before: For a single action, an expectation under π can sometimes be estimated from actions sampled under μ using importance weight π(a|s)/μ(a|s), provided μ covers π's support. Full trajectories can require products of ratios and additional treatment of state-distribution differences, making variance severe. Some off-policy algorithms instead use value-learning objectives with their own assumptions. A one-step ratio does not magically turn every stale trajectory into an unbiased estimate of every desired quantity.
issues.after: For a single action at a fixed state, an expectation under π can sometimes be estimated from actions sampled under μ using importance weight π(a|s)/μ(a|s), provided μ covers π's support. A full-trajectory likelihood ratio is the product of per-step action ratios when the initial-state and environment dynamics are shared; it already accounts for the induced state-distribution change, but its variance can be severe. Methods that avoid that product need their own corrections or assumptions. A one-step ratio does not turn every stale trajectory into an unbiased estimate of every desired quantity.
issues.reason: A full trajectory ratio already corrects the induced state distribution because shared environment factors cancel.

A faster attention kernel cannot accelerate input preprocessing or FFNs beyond the fraction of time they leave available.

It reduces memory traffic and intermediate storage through a hardware-aware schedule. Benefits depend on shapes, device support, masking, dtype, and the selected kernel. Test numerical closeness within appropriate tolerances rather than demanding bitwise identity. Also distinguish prefill from single-token decoding, whose bottlenecks differ. A faster attention kernel does not speed up preprocessing or FFNs; end-to-end speedup is bounded by the fraction of runtime spent in attention.

issues.before: A VAE's reconstruction term is a negative log-likelihood under p(x|z). Mean squared error corresponds to a Gaussian observation model under particular variance assumptions; binary cross-entropy corresponds to Bernoulli observations. These choices express different assumptions about the data. Replacing one with another or changing its reduction changes the optimization problem. The decoder's output activation and the numerical loss function must agree, such as using logits with a stable logits-based binary loss.
issues.after: A VAE's reconstruction term is a negative log-likelihood under p(x|z). Mean squared error corresponds to a Gaussian observation model under particular variance assumptions; binary cross-entropy is a Bernoulli negative log-likelihood for binary observations. Applying the same expression to continuous intensities in [0,1] does not by itself define a normalized continuous likelihood; a continuous Bernoulli, for example, needs an additional parameter-dependent normalizer. These choices express different assumptions about the data. Replacing one with another or changing its reduction changes the optimization problem. The decoder's output activation and the numerical loss function must agree, such as using logits with a stable logits-based binary loss.
issues.reason: The Bernoulli likelihood interpretation requires binary data; continuous intensities need a proper observation distribution.
issues.origin: Claude baseline suggestion independently validated by OpenAI

issues.before: Suppose the conditional prediction is c and the unconditional prediction is u. The form u+w(c−u) equals c+s(c−u) when w=1+s. Thus a displayed value of three in one convention can correspond to two in another; comparing raw labels would describe different algorithms as identical.
issues.after: Ho and Salimans use (1+w_p)c − w_p u, where c and u are conditional and unconditional predictions. This article uses u+w_a(c−u), so w_p=w_a−1. The paper's w_p=0 corresponds to w_a=1 here, both yielding c. Likewise, this article's scale three matches the paper's scale two.
issues.reason: Make the cited paper's scale convention explicit rather than warning only about unspecified alternatives.

limitations: This is a technical content audit, not proof that every scientific claim is error-free or that cited results generalize beyond their assumptions.
Primary sources were inspected for the relevant claims, not reproduced experimentally. No model was trained; no GPU kernels, PyTorch API examples, distributed jobs, or benchmark suites were executed.

The 73 executed numerical checks are small JavaScript calculations, not neural-network validation. Their descriptions identify what was actually tested; broader reasoning and formula derivations were reviewed statically.
PyTorch 2.14 documentation URLs were successfully opened during this review. The content makes no claim that this pinned version is the newest release.

The rendered Spinning Up policy-optimization page could not be fetched reliably and last returned HTTP 429; its official repository source was successfully read. Existing rendered-page references remain valid canonical citations but their immediate availability was not established.

The direct Boyd textbook PDF and a Sutton/Barto book fetch failed during research; neither failed resource is required by the final additions. The official Boyd lecture PDF and official Spinning Up documentation/source were used instead.
Paper-reading examples are original instructional analyses. Their hypothetical scenarios are not claimed to be experiments or numerical results reported by the cited papers.
Cross-module prerequisite IDs were validated, but this subagent did not audit the full prose of modules 01–08. Other agents own those articles.

The expanded Claude pass reviewed the full enriched snapshot using reasoning only. OpenAI checked its five findings against sources, applied four scoped clarifications, and rejected the conditional PyTorch-link concern after reopening all six URLs.

The newly added original Higgins et al. β-VAE OpenReview reference displayed browser verification. Attribution and objective support were confirmed in the authors' primary follow-up; full text of the originating paper was not fetched.

The authors' 2018 primary paper explicitly attributes β-VAE to Higgins et al. (reference 15) and presents the original weighted objective separately from its capacity extension. The canonical OpenReview forum/PDF returned browser verification; this retrieval limitation is recorded rather than claiming full-text access to that original paper.

Used Generative Adversarial Networks, the linked arXiv listing's title, consistently in the prose and references of 09-09 and 12-06. Both earlier title variants were valid; this is consistency rather than a corrected scientific claim.

Verified POPE's stated 1:1 ratio of ground-truth to nonexistent objects. Rewrote the hypothetical shortcut example to state POPE's balanced design and the always-no baseline of 50%, while retaining precision/recall/yes-rate diagnostics.
